props.title: The Best Years of Our Lives
props.initialSlug: Three veterans navigate rocky postwar homecomings

sections.content: The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) revolutionized how Hollywood portrayed war's aftermath. Director William Wyler, fresh from documenting WWII himself, crafted an unflinching look at three veterans struggling to readjust to civilian life. The film's groundbreaking authenticity came partly from casting real-life disabled veteran Harold Russell, who lost both hands in the war. This choice preceded the method acting era of On the Waterfront (1954) and stands in stark contrast to earlier sanitized war pictures like Wings (1927). movies.title: The Best Years of Our Lives
movies.slug: Three WWII veterans struggle to readjust to civilian life in this Academy Award-winning drama

sections.content: The film's influence echoes through decades of post-war cinema. The Deer Hunter (1978) mirrors its multi-character study of homecoming trauma, while Stop-Loss (2008) updates the narrative for Iraq War veterans. The innovative deep-focus cinematography by Gregg Toland (fresh from Citizen Kane (1941)) allows viewers to read multiple characters' reactions simultaneously, creating a documentary-like realism that influenced Italian Neorealism.

Wyler's masterpiece broke new ground in depicting PTSD before the term existed. Its honest portrayal of alcoholism, marital strain, and unemployment among veterans created a template followed by films like Last Flag Flying (2017) and Thank You for Your Service (2017). The film's nearly three-hour runtime was unprecedented for a domestic drama, paving the way for serious, extended examinations of American life. movies.title: The Messenger
movies.slug: Two soldiers must notify families of military casualties while dealing with their own war trauma

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond war-themed movies. Its realistic portrayal of American family life influenced everything from The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit (1956) to Revolutionary Road (2008). The character of Homer Parrish, played by Harold Russell, opened doors for authentic portrayals of disability in cinema, though Hollywood took decades to build on this progress.
